name: Winter arc lock-in
tagline: Five habits to lock in before the cold gets to your hair.
image_alt: Chunky two-strand twists parted off the hairline, resting over one shoulder.
description: Five winter hair-care habits: a scalp routine worth sticking to, a gentler cleanser, lipids and sealed ends, warm conditioning, and getting your levels checked. Built for length retention.
intro: Cold air outside, dry heat inside, hats and scarves rubbing your hair all day. Winter is a lot. This plan is five habits to go all in on this season, one at a time. The goal isn't a new head of hair by spring. It's keeping the hair you grow.

causes.title: Why winter is hard on hair
causes.intro: None of this is your fault. It's just the season.
items: Cold air holds less moisture, and indoor heating dries it out even more.
Hair and scalp can feel drier and tighter than usual.
Fabric rubbing against your hair all day.
Friction roughens the surface of the strand and tangles ends. Satin or silk lining makes a difference.
Hot water feels amazing when it's freezing out.
It can leave scalp and hair drier. Lukewarm for hair is kinder.
Less sleep, more stress, a heavier schedule.
Your body and your hair feel it too, which is why the last lock is a check-up.

routine.title: The five habits for winterizing your hair care
routine.intro: Start with one habit, get comfortable, then add the next.

washes.title: Lock it in
steps: Protective styles, buildup, sweat and dry air all land on your scalp first. Keep it clean, notice itching early, and add a leave-on serum with caffeine, green tea or peptides.

steps.dek: Healthy-looking hair starts with a scalp routine worth sticking to.
steps.image_alt: Hands holding a dropper bottle of The Ordinary Multi-Peptide Serum for Hair Density against dark wood.

blocks.title: Six scalp ingredients, decoded
items: The most studied of the six. Early research looks promising for follicle activity.
Antioxidants being studied for scalp health and follicle signalling.
A peptide plus red clover extract, for fuller-looking hair.
A plant complex with a green-tea-derived ingredient, aimed at density.
A peptide with apigenin and oleanolic acid, for density formulas.
Used in anti-hair-fall formulas. It is not minoxidil.

use: The INKEY List Caffeine Stimulating Scalp Treatment
L'Oréal Paris Elvive Fall Resist Aminexil Serum

deeper.title: How to apply a scalp serum
deeper.sub: And how to judge a formula

blocks.text: The evidence varies, so judge the whole formula, not one headline ingredient.
Part your hair into sections, apply to the scalp as the label says, and massage in with your fingertips. Regular use beats a big dose once in a while.

steps.lockin: Make scalp care part of the routine, not something you remember when your hair acts up.
steps.note: Heavier shedding that won't stop, or patchy thinning? See a dermatologist.
steps.quote: Consistency is more useful than a generous amount once in a while.

steps: Winter is no excuse to skip wash day, but it is a reason to wash gently. About once a week is a good starting point for textured hair, including under braids and twists.

steps.dek: Clean hair is healthy hair. Yes, even in winter.
steps.image_alt: Washing coily hair at a bathroom sink, lather worked into the scalp with fingertips.

blocks.title: Sulfate-free doesn't mean gentle.
paras: Strength comes from the whole cleanser blend, not one word on the front of the bottle.

deeper.title: When to clarify, and when flakes aren't dryness

blocks.text: Wash the scalp, not the lengths
Shampoo in sections at the scalp and let the lather rinse through your lengths. No piling hair on top of your head.
If hair feels coated or products stop working, use a clarifying shampoo, then a conditioner or mask to bring back slip.
Persistent itching, redness or flaking can be seborrheic dermatitis. More oil won't fix it; a dermatologist can suggest a treatment shampoo.

steps.lockin: A gentle shampoo for every wash, a clarifier for when buildup calls for it.
link: Cleanser levels, from gentlest to strongest
steps.label: A level 1 shampoo to try
steps.quote: Buildup doesn't become beneficial just because your hair is tucked away.

steps: Give your strands their lipids, and seal those ends
Winter hair's biggest enemy is friction. Condition for slip and softness, then seal your ends so they stop catching on each other all week.

steps.dek: This is where your conditioning routine gets serious.
steps.image_alt: Hands holding a jar of Briogeo Don't Despair, Repair! deep conditioning mask against dark wood.

items: Slip and softness, on wash day.
A light coat on your ends that cuts friction all week.

blocks.title: Four ways to seal
items: The most slip. Smooth a little over your leave-in, on the last few inches.
The lightest. A few drops if richer products weigh you down.
Coconut oil can get inside the hair and reduce protein loss, so it's also a good pre-wash treatment.
Petrolatum and mineral oil: classic for very dry ends and twists. Warm a little in your palms.

deeper.title: What's inside a strand, and what makes a great conditioner
deeper.sub: Lipids, ceramides and the formula behind slip

blocks.text: Hair is held together partly by lipids, including the cell membrane complex between its cells. Heat, colour and everyday wear damage them, making hair rougher and easier to break.
Ceramides are lipids too, but the whole conditioner matters more: fatty alcohols for texture, cationic conditioners and silicones for slip, oils for softness.
Pick one, apply it after your leave-in, and reapply when your ends start to feel rough.

steps.lockin: Slip first, then a seal. Two parts of one strategy against friction.
steps.quote: Think of sealing as giving each strand a thin protective jacket.

steps: Stand the closed bottle or tub in warm water for a few minutes, or condition under a thermal cap. Thick formulas spread more easily, and wash day feels like a treatment.

steps.dek: Make wash day feel like a treatment, not a chore.
steps.image_alt: Wearing a pink thermal heat cap over the hair while conditioning, in a pink robe.

deeper.title: Why warmth helps (and when it doesn't need to)

blocks.text: Heat can help some oils, like coconut oil, get inside the hair. But most conditioner ingredients work on the surface, and that's fine: a smoother surface means less friction.
Skip heat if your scalp is irritated or sensitive.

steps.lockin: Gentle warmth, product directions followed, and let the formula do its job.
steps.label: The heat-cap edit
steps.quote: Not every conditioning ingredient needs to penetrate the hair to be useful.

blocks.title: Three ways to add warmth
items: Stand the closed tub in warm water for a few minutes. Never microwave it.
Gentle, steady warmth while you condition. Follow the product's timing.
Warm a little coconut oil in a water bath and apply to lengths before shampoo. Never hot.

steps: Sometimes the missing piece isn't a product. Nutrition, thyroid, hormones, illness and stress can all change shedding, so if yours has changed, talk to your doctor about bloodwork.

steps.dek: Some answers aren't in your bathroom cabinet.

blocks.title: Tests your doctor may consider
items: Your iron stores. Many hair specialists look for about 40–70 ng/mL when shedding is a concern.

blocks.title: Test first. Iron especially.
paras: Too much iron can be harmful, and extra vitamins aren't a shortcut to growth. Only a test shows what you need.

deeper.title: Ferritin: the 40–70 ng/mL range
deeper.sub: What the number means, and what it doesn't

blocks.text: Many hair specialists look for a ferritin of about 40–70 ng/mL when shedding is a concern. That's well above the 12–15 ng/mL cutoff labs often use to diagnose iron deficiency, so a result marked "normal" can still be worth discussing.
It's a range to talk through with your doctor, not a guarantee of growth, and not a reason to take iron on your own. Too much iron can be harmful.

steps.lockin: Shedding changed? Talk to your doctor before you add another supplement.
steps.image_alt: Hands lifting long dark curls away from the parting at the scalp.
steps.quote: Taking more than you need isn't a shortcut to longer or thicker hair.

between.title: Every day this winter
groups: Check your ends. If they feel rough, add a little leave-in or finishing serum.
Choose satin- or silk-lined hats when you can.
Wearing a scarf? Add a satin layer underneath to cut rubbing.
Keep protective styles comfortable, with no extra tension around your hairline.
Satin bonnet or a silk or satin pillowcase.
Keep styles loose enough to avoid tension.
Tuck exposed ends into a protective style or cover them.
Give your scalp some attention, especially after hats or a workout.

trouble.title: If something feels off
items: Dry winter air is a common cause, but flaking and itching can have other causes too. If it doesn't settle, ask a doctor or dermatologist.
Go back to a moisturising conditioner and warm it up. Check for buildup before you add anything.
See your doctor. Bring up vitamin D, iron and ferritin, and anything else going on with your health, medicines or stress.
Look at friction first: hats, scarves, collars. Satin lining helps.

end.title: The winter hair-care lock-in
notes: You don't need a new head of hair by spring. You need a routine that keeps the hair you're growing.
The real winter hair flex isn't just growth. It's retention.
